subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS    STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE RESPECTING HAL BANKS
MR. WOOLLIAMS    STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE RESPECTING HAL BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege affecting the hon. members of this house. My question of privilege is on two grounds, and refers to a statement made yesterday by the Minister of Justice with reference to Mr. Banks.
My first point of privilege is that the minister misinformed the house with reference to the issuance of a warrant and the date of a warrant for Mr. Banks' arrest. My second point of privilege is that the minister said it was against public policy to disclose those facts. In answer to my point of privilege yesterday and to questions asked by the Leader of the Opposition, myself, the hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Winnipeg North, the Minister of Justice, when pressed after several questions, replied as follows, as reported on page 4354 of yesterday's Hansard:
Well, Mr. Speaker, a number of those questions have already been answered. The charge was laid in Montreal. It was laid against Mr. Banks. It was laid on October 23, and on October 31 search warrants were issued arising out of these charges. In so far as the last part of the question is concerned, I do not believe it is in the public interest to give that information.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us deal with the facts. Since listening to the Minister of Justice yesterday I have had the courthouse records checked. I say that with regard to the major point on which we sought to get information yesterday, the question of the date, the Minister of Justice misinformed the house.
Here are the facts, as gained from searching the courthouse records. On October 23 an information was laid by Joseph MacLeod, R.C.M.P., that Ernest Paul Carsh, Eldon Richardson alias Jack Richardson, Hal Banks, and Jack Caspar of California and other persons unnamed did conspire to commit bodily harm.
May I pause here. Several days ago we asked to be told the date of the alleged offence. The Minister of Justice stated it was around August, 1957. According to the charge it was a continuing offence from January 1 to August 31, 1957.
28902-5-280i
And now we come to the most important point. According to the answer, the search warrant was issued on October 31. On what date was the warrant for arrest issued? This may seem to be quibbling about time, but time is of the essence when a man such as Banks is at large charged with a criminal offence. On October 23 a warrant was issued for their arrest. Search warrants were issued by Judge Trottier for the homes of Carsh, Banks and Richardson and for S.I.U. headquarters. In brief, on October 23 a warrant was issued for the arrest of Banks. In other words, at the time Banks was here on parliament hill there was a warrant issued for his arrest, but it was not executed.
As to the other warrants of October 31, let me explain the circumstances briefly. On that date search warrants were issued. For what? They had nothing to do with the conspiracy charge. In this regard I say the Minister of Justice misinformed the house. On October 31 search warrants were issued. No charges were laid. They were in respect of the alleged violation of section 268 of the Canada Shipping Act, enticing to desert. Involved as subjects of the allegation were 16 sailors of the motor vessel Franquelin, Montreal registry. Nothing was found at Banks' home. In other words, at the time the charge was laid on October 23 there was a warrant issued for the arrest of Banks. The Minister of Justice left the impression that this warrant was not issued until October 31.

speechtext:
That is the only charge that has been laid against Banks to date, although other charges against Banks and certain other officers of the S.I.U. arising out of the Norris report and the recent illegal strike are being considered.
At the same time that the charge was laid against Banks, similar charges were laid against men by the names of Richardson and Carsh. On Friday, November 1 and Saturday, November 2 search warrants relating to such charges and to possible conspiracy to contravene the Canada Shipping Act were executed upon various premises, including Banks' residence and the S.I.U. halls in Montreal, Toronto and Thorold. In some instances the search warrants were taken out at or about the same time that the charges were laid against Banks, Richardson and Carsh, and in some instances just before the searches were executed.
Warrants for the arrest of Banks, Richardson and Carsh were issued contemporaneously with or immediately following the taking and swearing of the informations relating to the charges. In the case of Banks such warrant, I have been informed by the special crown prosecutor, was executed at two o'clock this afternoon and Mr. Banks was put under arrest at that time.
These warrants were not executed immediately upon being taken out.

subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS    STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE RESPECTING HAL BANKS
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS    STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE RESPECTING HAL BANKS
speechtext:
My hon. friends ask why, and I think they have a right to know why. That arises out of the question put by the hon. member as to why the warrant was not executed when Mr. Banks was here on parliament hill. It is my recollection, though I may be wrong-I will have to check-that

they were not issued until after that time. They were issued some days later.
In answer to the question which was put, the first concern of the government in the matter of the strike was to get the men back to work. Having got the men back to work and having got the ships and the grain moving, the next concern of the government was to keep the men on the job on the ships. I thought, rightly or wrongly, having regard to these circumstances, that when the trustees were entering upon their duties as trustees of the union I should not, when one department was acting in one direction, attempt to interfere with the duties of those trustees. That explains the reason we did not proceed. I did not consider it would be good timing at that time. As minister I was bound to take into account the whole situation, and with all respect to members of the house I have taken that situation into consideration.
Having regard to the fact that the matter has been disposed of in so far as the arrest at least of one person at two o'clock is concerned, I should think, Mr. Speaker, that that disposes of the question of privilege.

subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS    STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE RESPECTING HAL BANKS
speechtext:
In view of the general interest in this matter I have allowed the discussion to go on a little longer than is perhaps justified. However, I am sure hon. members will not object if I call to their attention Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 104, subsection 5:
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity. If he is not so satisfied he may allow the member to make a statement with a view to ascertaining whether or not a prima facie case can be made out. The right of making complaint of a breach of privilege is open to any member of the house, and, even if an individual member alone is affected, is not confined to that member.
Then if we go to citation 113, which it may be useful to recall at this time, hon. members will find the following:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters that should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the house. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy.
Then it goes on, and the point at issue is this, and I quote from the same citation 113:
But a dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
It seems to me that those words apply to the present situation almost word for word.

I am sorry, but I do not see a prima facie case of privilege in the matter raised by the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that on behalf of the government of Canada I have this morning signed a long term wheat agreement with the government of Poland. In connection with the negotiation of the agreement it has been my pleasure to welcome to Ottawa Mr. Trampczynski, the Polish minister of foreign trade. Mr. Trampczynski, who I am pleased to say is in the gallery this afternoon, signed the agreement on behalf of his government.
The agreement is for a period of three years, during which Poland will purchase and Canada will supply 1.2 million metric tons of Canadian wheat, that is about 44 million bushels, for shipment in the following quantities: In the first year of the agreement, 400,000 metric tons, of which a minimum of 200,000 tons shall be shipped between the opening of navigation and July, 1964. In the second and third years of the agreement a combined total of 800,000 metric tons in such yearly amounts as the buyer chooses, provided that the quantity purchased in each of these years shall not be less than 300,000 metric tons.
Purchases under this agreement will be facilitated by the extension of credit arrangements under the Export Credits Insurance Act providing, as has been customary in all the transactions with Poland, for payment over three years. Poland has been a regular customer for Canadian wheat, having made its first purchases in 1955 under credit arrangements. Since that year Poland has purchased wheat from Canada annually, and these purchases have totalled 73 million bushels. The important new agreement signed today is evidence of the desire of both governments to provide for the continuation of this trade on a regular basis.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians I should like to join with the minister in welcoming the minister of trade of Poland to our country, where he put into formal arrangements the long term agreement covering the continuing trade that has been going on for a number of years.
Since 1955.

However, I would like to make one or two observations, and the first is that this is the second occasion we have had such an announcement made outside the
Sale of Wheat to Poland house. It is understood that when parliament is in session, announcements like this should be made to the members of parliament first, but the minister is new and I know he has to learn.
The second point I want to make is that I trust and understand from the announcement, although it was not too clear on this point, that the price arrangement will be the traditional one, namely that the price will be set during the term of the first contract and each succeeding contract will be negotiated at the price existing at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house and the people of Canada generally will be pleased that the Canadian wheat board has been able to secure another agreement for the sale of wheat. The prairie farmers are now receiving the benefit of the long years they struggled to get a wheat board as the sole marketing agency for handling their grain.
If anything were needed to prove the value of such an agency, I think the events of recent months have gone far to do that. I believe it was Winston Churchill who once spoke about the new world setting out to redress the balance of the old.

speechtext: It was Canning.

I think in our case the communist world is setting out to redress the financial imbalance of the western world, and we can be very thankful that the large purchases from east of the iron curtain are going to help Canada move this year toward a balance of payments.

Mr. Speaker, this is another of the wheat deals that have been announced in the house recently, and we are happy to see a further sale of 44 million bushels of Canadian wheat. It is worthy of note in this particular case that the arrangements between the Canadian government and the Polish government back in 1955 actually set the stage for credit arrangements that have been so useful to the Canadian wheat board.
There is just one further thing I wish to mention at this stage, and that is that there is a problem in eastern Canada respecting feed grain. I hope the minister responsible for announcements by the Canadian wheat board, and others across the way, will take this matter under consideration at once, refer it to the committee on agriculture and colonization, and get that committee active so that we may make certain there will be adequate stocks in position, and at a reasonable price, for the ensuing months.

Sale of Wheat to Poland [Translation]	PUBLIC SERVICE

Mr. Speaker, this new sale of Canadian wheat to Poland gives proof that several countries are interested in securing some of this important wheat production we have in Canada.
It seemed to me, as I heard the Minister of Agriculture make the announcement with respect to the agreement signed this morning between the Polish government and the Canadian government for the sale of 44 million bushels of wheat, that he could also have informed us of a meeting between himself, the officials of his department and eastern farmers with a view to reaching an agreement with eastern farmers for selling wheat to them under similar terms.
There is another very important point. When the Minister of Agriculture meets delegations made up of visitors from foreign lands, he could perhaps take this opportunity to point out to them that we have in eastern Canada surpluses of apples, potatoes, wool and lumber. We even have gold and copper we could export, and then steel, milk and foodstuffs. Why not offer those buyers, at the same time, the things that are available in Canada?
I am merely urging the Minister of Agriculture to consider the field of agriculture not only in terms of wheat but also in terms of Canadian products in general.
We sincerely approve of this new wheat sale to Poland, but, as I said, the same opportunities should be given to eastern farmers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Maurice Lamonlagne (Presidenl of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I promised the hon. member for Danforth and the hon. member for Calgary North that I would make a statement this week with respect to the implementation of certain recommendations of the royal commission on government organization. The government's intentions have already been made known with respect to the development of a common procurement agency, as recommended by the royal commission, and the realignment of duties and functions affecting the printing bureau. This present statement covers a considerable number of additional recommendations on which decisions have now been made.
The additional recommendations of the royal commission which have now been approved cover a wide range of subjects dealt with in the first three volumes of the report. They include recommendations dealing with financial management; personnel management; purchasing and supply; transportation; telecommunications; printing and publishing; the "make or buy" problem; legal services; economic and statistical services; public information services; education services; health services; lending, guaranteeing and insuring; post office; and other services. As the full list of recommendations now approved, including those covered by this latest decision, is relatively long, numbering more than 60, I wonder if the house would agree that instead of reading them all I might table the list. My office will be ready to provide this list to all those hon. members who may ask for it. An opportunity will be presented, in the consideration of the estimates for 1963-64, to discuss the details of these recommendations if any member wishes to do so.
I should point out, of course, that this list does not by any means represent all the recommendations made by the royal commission under the headings I have mentioned. It does represent those recommendations which the government, under the procedures it has established, has been able to review to date, and with respect to which the government has indicated its agreement in principle. Having accepted them in principle, the government will now work toward their implementation.
The process of review of the recommendations of the royal commission is continuing and, as further decisions are made by the government, the house will be informed from time to time.
Does the house give consent to the tabling of this list?
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. gentleman assumed the position of President of the Privy Council and took over the administration of the bureau of government organization, it was felt by many that he had little enthusiasm for the recommendations of this commission. Today we have had a list of generalized items, but it is impossible to say how far the government has gone. On its face it appears that the purpose for which this commission was set up, namely to bring an end to waste, extravagance, duplication of services and red tape, has been lost sight of by this government.
The hon. gentleman mentioned that some 60 items are dealt with. Those will have to be studied. Having regard to the experience of the past it may be a list barely touched in any way. I can only say that on the basis of the experience we have had, this government is giving but lukewarm support to the recommendations which were made, which were designed to bring about the changes I mentioned a moment ago as well as to end the governmental administrative jungle that has accumulated through the years and has mushroomed since the second world war.
It is now clear, on the basis of the experience we have had, that except for minor changes the commission report in the main is going to be pigeonholed. These items which are referred to are, generally speaking, the insignificant recommendations. There are some recommendations which naturally will not be accepted, but I would say to the minister that in mentioning that 60 cases have been considered, from the experience we have had to date the dribbles have been proceeded with by the government but the major reasons for the recommendations and the recommendations themselves have been neglected.
However, we will have an opportunity of looking over this list in detail when the estimates are before the house. In the meantime I think Canadians as a whole will feel that this is just another example of 60 days of promises without carrying those promises into effect. What has been done is merely to touch the edge and to pretend that the recommendations are being carried out.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement was almost useless to us in that he did not give us any kind of framework on which the government is approaching this matter. He has given us a list. We will have to look at the list to see whether it contains anything significant. He gave us no indication as to what estimates
Implementation of Glassco Report will be affected; I suppose these changes will apply to almost every department. Does this mean that we will have to hare from one department to another on the estimates in order to find out what is going on, or is the government prepared to make some provision when discussing the estimates to enable us to quiz the President of the Privy Council and Mr. Davidson, who is advising him, and get the picture once and for all of all the changes relating to this royal commission? That is all we have to say at this time.

Mr. Speaker, we are glad to see that the government is taking some action toward clearing up the accumulated government jungle which has gathered during the last few years. We hope that this is a sign of better things to come.

Mr. Speaker, I think it requires quite a stretch of the imagination for us to be able to congratulate the government following the statement just made by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne), since it was devoid of meaning and had no other purpose than to announce something about which we had not been previously advised. It had to do with some sort of reform.
We would rather wait before offering our congratulations, since before throwing bouquets, we want to know why. Otherwise, we might be inclined to throw in the vase also.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked me to comment on the statement made by Mr. Arthur E. Beeby, executive vice president of Salada Foods, having to do with sugar price fluctuations. The hon. member referred to Mr. Beeby as having said in effect that "the recent series of increases in sugar prices cannot be explained on the basis of supply and demand, that there is no world sugar shortage", and that as a major Canadian buyer of refined sugar he was forced to the conclusion that the rise in cost of this staple food item on world markets did not result from demand but from speculation.
I asked the director of research in the combines investigation branch to inquire into this situation. The director communicated with Mr. Beeby and he has advised me of the following and has also obtained the permission of Mr. Beeby to disclose what I am about to say.
In his statement Mr. Beeby was not alleging any fact that in his opinion discloses a breach of any provision of the Combines Investigation Act. He also did not purport to suggest that the government can adopt any measure that can control or influence the price of sugar in the world market; nor did he suggest any step that the government might take to affect the domestic price of sugar in Canada. He stated that his purpose in issuing the statement was to warn Canadians of the fact that as a manufacturer his company is faced with rising sugar costs, which he considers Canadians are helpless to control and which will inevitably affect the price of his company's products.
This statement was reread by the director to Mr. Beeby, and he said that he agreed with it.

LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night I had completed about half my speech, but at closing time there are not nearly so many members in the house as I find now. Rather than see them all move out in such droves, perhaps I should appeal to

Unemployment Measures Lacking them in the language Shakespeare used in the first scene of Hamlet, when Bernardo said:
Sit down awhile,
And let us once again assail your ears.
That are so fortified against our story-
I shall try to keep my remarks as brief as may suit the occasion, Mr. Speaker. I think I dealt pretty generally last night with what I believed to have been the pattern of the provisions the government undertook in dealing with the problems of unemployment. In essence, I think we said that the country had been changing from an agricultural country to a manufacturing one, and that we had the attendant problem of training people, finding markets, finding money, and all that was involved in such sweeping changes. I referred to the many dramatic actions by the former government. If we refer to the subamendment we find that it reads in this way:
-and also the failure of the government to propose any plans for the fundamental economic and social changes required to deal with the chronic and growing problem of unemployment caused by automation and technological change.
I outlined, Mr. Speaker, the steps taken by the previous government, which were fundamental, in relation to the economy and the social strata of the country. Certainly we went beyond what was thought daring a few years ago. The government recognized the need to create an economic atmosphere to get private enterprise to flourish. We went beyond that. We found many fields in which the government had to give the lead, had to provide the money, had to take steps to find new ways to push private enterprise into new methods of doing things.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that no one in this house would take me amiss if I were to say that we could add to that subamendment proposed by the New Democratic party the words "similar to the type of legislation brought in by the previous government." Considering how far we have gone, the wording of this subamendment cannot, by any reasonable stretch of the imagination, be taken to suggest socialism. We know that the concepts of government and of the needs of the country are changing so much that this subamendment merely describes the sort of bold, imaginative action taken by the previous government. I trust that all who are acutely aware of the problem of unemployment in this country will have no hesitation in backing it.
I know from having observed what has happened that a bond of friendship seems to have sprung up between the present Liberal administration and the Social Credit group. There is a strong suspicion in the house that they are going to be anxious to sustain the government. I know, on occasion, how pleased

the government has been to find that little group of friends. I do not want to burden Shakespeare with the entire responsibility for my speech, but there are some words that appear in "Timon of Athens" which I thought would be appropriate when the Liberals are considering their friends the Social Crediters. These lines are as follows:
O! what a precious comfort 'tis, to have so many, like brothers, commanding one another's fortunes.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I remember when the Social Crediters supported us, and when the New Democratic party supported us. When they thought they detected a rift in the Conservative party they thought it might be the appropriate moment to strike. They hoped that the trouble in our party might lead to further gains for theirs. They were sadly mistaken. Certainly this time I believe they must think carefully before they strike so recklessly again.
I know no member in this house can look at the actions taken by the present Liberal government and feel satisfied that any strong action has been taken against unemployment. Perhaps the words used by the Secretary of State on April 22 of this year, when the Liberals took office, were prophetic and reflected the real attitude of the members of this government. When he was asked what his feelings were, he said it was nice to be employed again after all those years of unemployment. I am sure we get the feeling that many members of the cabinet believe they have now licked their unemployment problem.
However, it is the unemployment problem of the country that requires action. Certainly there have been many dramatic experiments, shall I say, in connection with the budget. I could have said "horrible experiments". We were looking for something exciting, but we had something quite exciting in a different way. I think it was the first time in history that we nearly had a hanging after a budget. It was not just the people of this country who wanted to hang the Minister of Finance, but the Liberal backbenchers as well. I think the Prime Minister wanted to hang him, too, because of the embarrassment he had caused. There is nothing about this government that would give any hon. member of this house confidence in it, or the belief that it is capable of introducing legislation or instituting programs that are going to meet this evergrowing problem.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Ontario, the best that can be said of this government is that they have had the good sense to follow much of our program. Whenever they failed to follow the Conservative program they did not get anything done. In so

far as the vote tonight is concerned, it is not a question of whether this party will vote against the government; it is a question of whether all opposition parties will vote together against the government.
I suggest they should. I know the amendment will cause considerable soul searching. However, I remind the small groups that they voted for what they thought were the interests of their parties the last time, no matter what it cost the country. They failed to serve the best interests of the country, because after that vote on February 5 last this country was saddled with this inadequate Liberal government. I am suggesting they do a little soul searching now to see if they cannot find it in their hearts to vote in the best interests of the country this time.
I should like to call once more upon Shakespeare, since his language is much better than mine, to explain the dilemma in which these small parties find themselves now. If the house will bear with me, I was not able to learn this well enough to give it without reading it. It is the famous speech by Hamlet, the soliloquy "To be or not to be," Shakespeare in a modern version:
To vote or not to vote; that is the question. Whether 'tis nobler of this house to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous government Or to take sides against a sea of bunglers And by opposing end them; to vote; to defeat; No more; and by a defeat to say we end The confusions and the many rude shocks Our economy is heir to, 'tis a consummation Devoutly to be wish'd. To vote; to defeat;
To defeat, to fight another time; ay there's the rub; For in that fight of ballots what defeats may come When we have shuffled off this parliament Must give us pause. There's the respect That makes travesty of such a life;
For who would bear the government of the time Their terrible mistakes Their contempt of parliament The death of hope, the laws delays Their insolence in office and the spurns Of good advice that these unworthies make When he himself might order bring With a bar vote. Who would Gordon bear But that the dread of something after dissolution The next election from whose wars some will not return
Puzzles the will, and makes us rather bear incompetents
That we have, than risk others that we know not of.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, I will get lots of good advice from various parts of the house that if I can only even borrow from language like that, then perhaps I have more future as a poet than a politician. I hope the Social Crediters, the Creditistes and the New Democratic party will all be voting with the Conservatives tonight against the government, and I may say that this matter of a mid-winter election strikes fear into the hearts of none stronger than it does into the Liberals. I had hoped at this stage to hear some advice
Unemployment Measures Lacking like Macbeth gave the witches, "Stop, you imperfect speakers, tell me more", but I am afraid my course is run.

speechtext:
No, I will permit questions at the end of my speech.
The trend has been downward in unemployment since that time, but what ought to be emphasized is that in the past six months total employment in Canada has shown a very strong advance. That is the important figure, and the most important statistic here is the year to year change. Unemployment as of September was 250,000, or 10,000 less than last year, and hon. gentlemen opposite seem to regard that as a very slight improvement. I regard it as a significant improvement, because it represents a complete reversal of the economic outlook that prevailed in Canada when this government took office. I hope to be able to say something more on this particular point later.
The statistics we have today may appear slight to hon. members opposite, but they underline two facts; that we reversed the unfavourable economic outlook, the unfavourable employment prospects that prevailed in Canada as of last April, and we improved the situation over last year.
It is true that Liberal members when in opposition introduced motions of non-confidence on the question of unemployment, but we presented those motions in periods of rising unemployment. Today and yesterday we have had motions put forward, not in a period of rising unemployment, but in a period of declining unemployment. That represents the difference between the two parties, unemployment rising under the Progressive Conservatives and decreasing under the Liberals.
In moving this amendment yesterday I hope the hon. member for Ontario will not think we will forget his performance, and the performance of his government, as they grappled unsuccessfully with the problem of unemployment throughout their whole period of office. Through this amendment he is asking us to visit with him, and with the other members of the former government, the scene of their major crime against the people of Canada, their failure to deal effectively with the problem of unemployment.
What was the performance of the former government? During that period there were excessively high levels of unemployment. Over the past five years unemployment averaged 6.6 per cent of the labour force all year around, and in that period of five years the winter rate was up to 10.1 per cent, while the summer average was 4.3 per cent of the labour force.
In the period from April 1, 1957 to March 31, 1963 the federal government, composed of hon. gentlemen opposite, paid out more than $300 million under the Unemployment Assistance Act, $300 million representing the


extent to which the unemployed of Canada were depending upon social assistance for a livelihood.
What happened to the unemployment insurance fund in that period when the Conservatives were in office? During that period the fund virtually disappeared, when the high levels of benefit payments represented the excessively high levels of mass unemployment. I do not intend to deal in detail with the benefit payments out of that fund each year, but they ranged from $385 million in 1958 to $513 million in 1961, all these figures indicating the excessively high levels of unemployment that prevailed in those years. That is the situation which this government faced when it entered office.
There have been recent improvements in the employment situation. The total employment picture has strengthened. Unemployment has decreased compared with the previous year and the prospects are that the Canadian economy will grow stronger in the months ahead. But the current labour market, with 250,000 persons unemployed, still reflects a high level of unemployment, a high level of unemployment which this government is determined to reduce, and with that object in mind has already put forward a number of major and effective programs to deal with the question. In the course of my remarks I will be referring to a number of these new and effective programs.
I point out this is a statistic which my hon. friend used to put on the record with regularity, that in September of this year employment in Canada totalled 6,565,000. Employment is greater by 180,000 than it was a year earlier. The Minister of Labour tends to be held responsible in this house and elsewhere for the whole problem of unemployment, and no doubt he does carry a full share of responsibility for this problem. But it ought to be apparent to all hon. members that a full range of policies is required to deal with unemployment, involving fiscal, monetary, trade and other relevant measures to stimulate employment and economic growth generally. I hope to be able to say more when introducing the estimates of the Department of Labour about my conception of the most effective way in which the Department of Labour can discharge its functions in co-ordination with other departments of government to deal with the problem of unemployment; but for the moment I am satisfied that the present government, in calling parliament together as quickly as possible following the election last April and introducing as quickly as possible major legislative measures to cope with unemployment, has kept faith with its determination, as expressed

to the electorate, that its foremost object on taking office would be to overcome unemployment.
Yesterday the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) spent most of his time talking about the municipal winter works incentive program. In fact, the main point in his speech was that the changes which had been made by the new government had served to reduce the effectiveness of this program. He stated that the changes made would curtail the activity of those who might be usefully employed in the winter months. We did introduce new ideas into this program. We announced our intention to carry out this program at the earliest date ever. We decided that in order to reach its maximum effectiveness it ought to be concentrated within a period of six months. We decided to increase the contribution for municipal buildings under this program by $50,000 and we increased the federal payroll cost from 50 to 60 per cent in designated areas and areas of high winter unemployment. Each of these improvements is known to members of the house.
Yesterday the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), in referring to this program, used the words-they were not his own words in the beginning-the "anaemic child of the government".

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That was the minister of external affairs.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Let us see how this child is doing under its new parents, Mr. Speaker. I have before me the forecast for the program this year, November 1, and the similar forecast for the program last year, October 15,
1962.	I want to put on the record these comparable statistics because they reveal how the child is doing. As of October 15, 1962, the applications approved were 1,450; on November 1, 1963, applications approved were 2,416. As of October 1962, estimated jobs involved 30,500; as of November 1, 1963, they involved 59,038. In October 1962 estimated man days of work to be provided, 1,650,000; this year the figure is 2,829,505. The estimated total of payroll costs last year was $25 million; this year the estimated total is $44 million. The estimated federal contribution last year was $12 million; this year it is $22 million. The estimated total cost of projects during the effective period last year was $83 million; this year it is $135 million. So these facts in themselves justify the efficacy of the improvements made by this government. They indicate the full health of the child under its new parentage, and they certainly present a strong justification for the defeat of this unsupported motion of non-confidence against this government.
The hon. member for Ontario spoke about winter unemployment. As I have indicated
Unemployment Measures Lacking already, we have strengthened and made more effective the municipal winter works incentive program, with good results. We have introduced a new bonus program, an incentive payment of $500 to the first purchaser of a winter-built house. This is a new program. The hon. member for Ontario calls it a gimmick. He said at one time in his speech that it will be ineffective, and at another time said it remains to be seen whether or not it will be effective. I believe this new experimental program will be effective. The response to date is encouraging. It will have a significant effect in increasing winter employment and in stabilizing employment opportunities in the construction industry. It is a new and effective program.
To meet the problem of unemployment this winter we have brought forward an accelerated winter construction program. This is an entirely new concept because it involves the bringing forward of projects not provided for in the regular estimates and for which justification exists on other grounds. The hon. member for Ontario asked how many new jobs $7 million would provide in this country of ours. Well, of course, he misses the point. This program does not apply to "this country of ours"; it applies to the designated areas, including 10 per cent of the paid workers of Canada, and also to areas of high winter unemployment, some of which are included already in the designated areas. These programs will be brought forward and undertaken this winter in these particular areas, and combined with other programs of the government this accelerated winter construction program will have a significant effect in reducing unemployment and in creating jobs this winter.
May I turn for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to another phase of the program of the government. We have designated certain parts of the country for special help. This is evidence of our policy to help areas in Canada most in need of help. It ought to be evident to hon. members of the house that any policy or incentive applied universally across the country will tend to make the economically strong parts of Canada stronger still. Such an approach will not help deal with areas of slow growth or high unemployment.
It has been said that this program of designation is discriminatory. Of course it is discriminatory. It is intended to be discriminatory in the sense of providing special assistance to areas of high unemployment and slow growth.
Yesterday the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) asked that special consideration be given to programs of this type. It is because we share that view that we have designated 35 areas in Canada as now eligible

Unemployment Measures Lacking for special stimuli under a new government program. A number of specific measures to promote development in these areas have already been announced by the government. They include tax exemptions for a three year period for new manufacturing and processing industries which locate in those areas. They include accelerated depreciation allowances on new machinery and equipment and an accelerated write-off of the capital cost of new industrial buildings in a five year period. These are the most powerful tax incentives ever offered by any Canadian government to assist in locating industries in areas of slow growth. Combined with the area development agencies and the new Department of Industry, these measures are bound to have a marked effect in accelerating growth, in reducing unemployment and in increasing total employment in these areas.
Besides these fiscal measures, provision has been made for the speeding up of government construction programs during the winter months and for an increase in the federal contribution to the municipal winter works incentive program from 50 per cent to 60 per cent. In addition, we have taken steps to strengthen the personnel of the national employment service. Surely, the effective use of manpower in Canada requires a strong national employment service equipped with the resources to make its contribution felt in the development of manpower policies. The former government applied austerity to the national employment service. We lifted that austerity program. The former government failed to maintain the national employment service at its proper establishment. We have added a large number of new positions to the service. For almost two years the national employment service in Canada was "frozen", and in April of this year there were vacancies to the number of 264 positions in the establishment of the service. This is how the government of Canada was treating the national employment service at a time of high unemployment, although the government of the United States, realizing how effective unemployment service could be in combating unemployment, had increased the total complement of its agency by more than 4,000. In order to make the services of the organization more effective we have added 362 new positions to the national employment service. We think this is a sound step because it will allow us to administer the new manpower policy and to establish the new programs we have undertaken, namely the older worker training program, the winter building program, and so on. We intend to support the national employment service and we have under consideration at the present time the
[Mr. MacEachen.l
recommendations of the Gill committee, with the further strengthening of that organization in mind.
I hope hon. gentlemen opposite will excuse me if I refer to the way in which the new government has strengthened the training program for the unemployed. It is true the former government did something in this field. I recognize that. We have taken steps to make the program more effective and we have extended for a further period the capital cost program under technical and vocational training, so that many more millions of dollars may be spent in building facilities and in adding to the training of our youth for the requirements of the sixties.
Now may I say a word about the incentive program for older workers. This program was designed in an effort to combat the prejudice against the re-employment of older workers. It is a new program. It is experimental and I think it fills a real need. As we all know, it is very hard for older workers who have been out of employment for a long time to re-establish themselves. Yet many of them are highly capable and have many years of useful working life ahead of them. Given an opportunity, they could bring their valuable qualities to the job-judgment, stability, less frequent absenteeism and reduced turnover and accident rate. The purpose of our program is to make it possible for employers to take these older workers and give them, if possible, training on the job or, at a minimum, to rehabilitate them to the point at which they become competitive in the labour market. If we succeed in doing this for any person I think it is a significant contribution to his future. The hon. member for Ontario says that those in charge of policing this program are having a difficult time-that they are encountering insurmountable difficulties. Well, the program has been in effect since Friday last, and on Monday the hon. member talks about facing insurmountable difficulties. That is hardly informed criticism. The hon. member for Ontario also said the program was a gimmick. That is his favourite description of a new program which he has not taken the trouble to understand or to study in detail. This is not a gimmick. It is the use of an incentive in a definite way to meet a definite problem.
As an indication of our determination to deal successfully and effectively with unemployment I should like to refer to the supplementary estimates, estimates D, which, in total, amount to $74 million, $60 million of which is being asked for to support the programs I have mentioned. By asking for this large amount-not a disproportionately large amount in terms of the problem to be solved

-the government has indicated the seriousness with which it regards the unemployment situation.
I do not intend to deal with the municipal loan fund. The hon. member for Ontario regards this as something which will create no jobs at all. We take a different attitude. We think this program, which is now in effect, will have a significant impact on employment opportunities. It is a new program and it deserves the support of all hon. members so that it may attain its maximum effect in reducing unemployment. We have established the Atlantic development fund. Surely, a fund of the amount of $100 million to be employed wholly within four provinces of Canada is bound to have an impact on employment in the immediate future. Then there is the provision in the supplementary estimates for a contribution by the federal government of 90 per cent toward the construction of the trans-Canada highway. This has already had a marked effect on employment. It is another new program, as is the municipal loan fund.
The newest program of all to which I should like to make reference with respect to its employment possibilities is the success of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) in negotiating this large sale of wheat and flour to Russia.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: We thought the wheat board did that.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Well, it has been done and it will have direct employment consequences. It is going to increase the number of men employed and the number of hours worked in the flour mills of this country. It will increase the number of men and the number of hours worked on the railways. It will increase the number of operators and the number of hours worked in connection with water transportation and handling of cargo at the ports. To some extent it will increase farm employment in Canada, especially in the western provinces. These are some of the direct effects of this particular sale of wheat and flour. The indirect effects will be substantial. Demand, generally, will be increased as a result of the increased spending power which will be generated within the economy. I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that this single sale will, in itself, add at least
20,000	or 25,000 additional jobs to the Canadian economy in the next 12 months.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In the eastern provinces?

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
In all parts of Canada- in the constituency of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) as well as of others in the maritimes, in Quebec and in the west. This is a universal program which
Unemployment Measures Lacking will increase jobs everywhere and its effects will become more apparent as time goes on.
May I turn for a moment to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in which he belaboured the government for its failure to propose any plan-I omit certain words-to deal with the problems of automation and technological change. I cannot accept the view set forth in the subamendment as being an accurate description of the policy of the government and the plan which it has already made clear with respect to meeting the problems posed by automation and technological change.
It seems to me we have taken two major steps. One has been in the field of training in industry. The hon. member for Ontario admitted yesterday that very little indeed has been done in the highly important field of training employees in industry. We have increased from 50 to 75 per cent the federal contribution to provincial costs in respect of training in industry. We think this will provide an additional stimulus to undertake the basic training of employees in industry.
It is a fact that in Canada today there are persons in the labour force whose skills are becoming obsolete and who are unable to acquire new skills because they do not have the basic education to allow them to do so. We are going to do something about this. We intend to do something about apprenticeship training and about retraining so that as one set of skills becomes obsolete a new set is acquired. That will be undertaken through this program.
The hon. member for Port Arthur may not have noticed that in the set of supplementary estimates tabled recently in the house provision has been made in a vote of the Department of Labour for a new manpower consultative service. In supplementary estimates A, page 12, he will notice that the government is asking the House of Commons for a special vote to provide for the establishment of manpower consultative service to assist in and encourage the establishment of manpower adjustment by employers and workers, and to authorize payments in accordance with agreements entered into with the approval of the governor in council by the Minister of Labour with provinces, employers and workers in respect of labour mobility and assessment incentives.
The purpose of this program is to cope for the first time in any country in this way with the problems of automation and technological change. We think that in putting forward this program which has been developed in the Department of Labour we are doing something in the way of pioneering

Unemployment Measures Lacking work. The principles of the program are simple but constructive. Appropriate plans will be developed at the plant level in advance of anticipated worker displacement. These plans will require advanced research and advanced assessment at the plant level, and this new manpower consultative service will assist employers and unions where they operate in a plant to assess prospective technological change, and will assist them to develop plans in order to meet the problems posed by technological change.
A direct effort will be made with government assistance to anticipate the need and to prepare for it in the way of programs to provide employment for displaced workers. At the same time, where transfer of workers displaced by technological change is not possible within the plant or within the community, re-employment incentives of another kind will be made available.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept the terms of the subamendment which belabour the government for its failure to deal with the problems of automation and technological change. We are taking two very important steps in this field and we think these steps will be effective and useful.
At the beginning of my remarks I stated in commenting on the present employment situation that the economic outlook that had prevailed in Canada last spring has been reversed, and that the advice available in the Department of Labour last spring projected not decreasing unemployment but increasing unemployment for September of this year. The former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario, said yesterday that the government of which he was a member had provided incentives to industry and that the present government is still riding on the effects of that impetus. That is an absurd contention and it ought to have been apparent to the hon. member for Ontario.
All I ask him is this: Did he ask his officials last March and April what the projections were for unemployment in September of this year? If he did he would have received precisely the same advice I received when I entered the Department of Labour, and that was that on the basis of the advice available the six month projection was that unemployment in September of 1963 would be greater than unemployment in September of 1962 and that the total advance in employment would not be as significant as it has turned out to be.
Therefore, whether we are riding on the impetus provided by the former government, which I doubt and deny, the fact is that the prospects known to members of the former government last spring called for higher unemployment this fall and a less rapid advance


in total employment. The outlook today is different. Employment over the year has increased from September to September by
180,000	and instead of an increase in unemployment as was projected there has been a decrease. That is in accordance with the advice I received on entering the department and in accordance with the facts that are generally known in the house today.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would ask hon. members to defeat these amendments because the present government called parliament together immediately to deal with the problems of unemployment and has brought forward a number of new and effective programs to do so. The policies of the new government have reversed the economic outlook that prevailed in Canada last April to the extent that there has been a marked increase in total employment and a significant decline in total unemployment. I also feel that the outlook for Canada is good. It will remain good and become stronger, provided the government is permitted to continue to implement the policies which it has begun.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I share with a good many members on this side of the house, a high regard for the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen). However, I must admit I was disappointed with the speech he just made. It seemed to me his remarks were rather political and very complacent. I do not blame him for making political remarks in the house, but I do not think this is the time or the occasion for complacency. The minister repeated to us, if I may borrow a phrase of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), a number of gimmicks that had been introduced by the government or, if the minister does not like that word, a number of incentives that have been brought into effect by the government. No doubt some of these are meritorious.
He also gave us figures relating to the expansion of employment. Of course we welcome the expansion of employment. However, he did not seem to recognize that there is a continuing need for a sufficient expansion of employment to provide full employment. The question is not whether we have expanded employment, which undoubtedly we have, but whether we have expanded employment to the extent where we can provide full employment in this country for all those able to work. This I say is the objective, and in that respect at least the government has failed so far. I listened carefully to the speech delivered by the minister, and I regret that he does not seem to have answered the rather searching questions put by one member from his own side of the house, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve). I refer to page 4374 of Hansard, where the hon. member is reported as saying this:
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that even though one knows the unemployment problem, its details, its various forms, as an hon. member of the opposition mentioned this afternoon, a basic decision has never been taken, namely whether governments.
Unemployment Measures Lacking federal and provincial, should interfere in the direction of the economy.
All kinds of solutions have been suggested, all aspects of the problem have been considered, but when one reads all these reports, one is always under the impression that there was a gap at a certain time and that the government was never able to make up its mind and really step into the economic field. I think that is the crux of the problem.
We could discuss ad infinitum the causes of unemployment and the solutions we think possible, but as long as governments-
I think he included this government.
-all of them, will not make up their minds to step in in order to stem unemployment and apply a policy of full employment, Canada will experience, as she has in the past, long periods of unemployment.
I ask the minister to pay heed to the words of his colleague from Iles-de-la-Madeleine. The hon. member went on to say this, and this is the last time I am going to avail myself of his speech for the purposes of my own:
As long as we go on thinking that private enterprise can solve the unemployment problem all by itself, that important public works, unemployment insurance and assistance will be able to help the jobless for some time, we will never solve definitely the full employment problem.
It is my submission that the minister, in his speech, failed to come to grips with the problem and indicate to this house the way the government accepted the responsibility which, quite rightly in my view, was put forward by the hon. member who spoke earlier in the debate. It seemed to me that when the minister referred, as he did, to the subamendment introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) he missed the import of it. I call attention to it. What we regret in the subamendment was the failure of the government to propose any plans for the fundamental economic and social changes required to deal with chronic and growing unemployment. The minister dealt with palliatives some of them good, some of them effective, but perhaps not to the degree he felt they were. He failed to tell us what proposals there were for the fundamental economic and social changes required, if we were to really deal with the situation.
I noticed that several other members who spoke in this debate took the opportunity presented by it to speak of the needs of their particular regions, and the problems of unemployment as they affected those regions. In this particular I want to follow the example of those who have preceded me in the debate, and take the opportunity to present to the house and to the government the urgent needs of the metropolitan area of the city of Toronto. All those needs are connected with this amendment, and if their solution

Unemployment Measures Lacking was taken seriously by the government it would put an end to the problem of unemployment where it is most acute, and that is in the large urban centres of Canada. If the government would deal with the problems of the metropolitan area of Toronto, I presume they would deal also with the problems of the other large urban centres. In so doing, they would go a long way toward tackling effectively this problem of unemployment.
What does the metropolitan area of Toronto most urgently need? It needs a public low cost housing program on a fairly large scale, a larger scale than we have ever had before. It urgently needs hospitals and hospital beds. It urgently needs rapid transit subways to deal with the burgeoning population and the expansion of suburban areas. These are not exclusively problems of the federal government. Indeed, primarily they may be the problems of other levels of government. However the leadership of the federal government is needed in each of these fields. Leadership, in these terms, would be an effective means of ending unemployment.
I suggest that the government has good reason to be concerned about these needs and should consider carefully the needs of the metropolitan area of Toronto. It was only in April, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal tide surged over that area. When the tide had subsided there were only two hon. members, my colleague from Danforth (Mr. Scott) and myself, who survived. I would have expected a very dynamic interest in the problems of the metro area on the part of this government.
What do we find? Despite the urgent requests of the mayor of Toronto and the members of the board of control, the Prime Minister announced that the effective date of the winter works program would be from November 1 to April 30. I will not use my own words to describe that decision, but Controller Lamport of the city of Toronto, a well-known Liberal, is reported as saying that the government had ignored Toronto's special problem in setting the deadline of April 30. He pointed out that although the national figures do show a decline in unemployment, and I must say it is a very small decline, the situation is worse in Toronto than it was a year ago. Taking the figures for September, he pointed out that unemployment had increased over 4 per cent during that period.
A gentleman by the name of A. V. Piggott, who was chairman of the employment advisory commission of Toronto, a well-known businessman who has also taken a leading part in the field of social welfare, is reported in the Toronto Star of October 25 as saying

that the situation in regard to unemployment was desperate. He said that there are now 100,000 to 125,000 jobs open in Toronto but the 125,000 unemployed cannot take those jobs because the openings were all for skilled workers. I dare say that is the experience of many members of this house. People come to ask for jobs, and the only jobs the member can find are for skilled personnel. These people however do not possess the basic skills required. I ask the government to note this. Mr. Piggott said he felt a terrible sense of urgency after visiting the United Kingdom and Europe and seeing what they are doing by way of retraining workers and by way of national economic planning. Mr. Piggott said he felt a terrible sense of urgency after realizing this situation, a sense of urgency not apparently shared by the government. However, I hope this motion will renew a sense of urgency on the part of the government today.
I was saying that the metropolitan area of Toronto urgently needs hospitals. I commend to the government an article in the Toronto Star of October 30 by the science editor who said that even if we built 10 new 200-bed hospitals the metro area would still be short of hospital space. In some suburbs like North York the present picture is so bad that, instead of the five beds per thousand residents, which is accepted as the proper standard, there is only half a bed per thousand residents in that area.
I know the government is giving consideration at the present time to the urgent requests of the metro executive to increase the government's contribution to the cost of adding the urgently needed hospital beds, as the province of Ontario and the metro council of Toronto have done. I urge the government to move quickly in increasing its contribution so that the urgently needed hospital construction be got under way soon, so that not only will the urgent need of beds for prospective patients be met but that winter unemployment can be substantially reduced.
I mentioned the subject of rapid transit construction, which I say is urgently needed. This is a major work in providing and creating employment. I would like to say in respect to this that plans, of course, are already in existence for the construction of rapid transit subways in the city of Toronto. I doubt if any people but the patient workers of the metropolitan area would put up with the sort of situation where it takes them an hour, and sometimes more than an hour, to get to their place of work in terribly overcrowded streetcars. This has a serious effect on their lives, and the construction of a subway would not only give them greater leisure but would add

further social benefits in the construction that would grow up around these more adequate transit facilities.
Again it may be said that this is a problem for the metropolitan area itself to deal with; but if the federal government would call the leaders of that large area into a conference with the leaders concerned with this matter in the provincial government and say, "We will accelerate that program and make it possible for you to go ahead with the program, and thus avoid spreading it out, as happens when the resources of the metropolitan area alone are to be relied on", this would have an immediate and very valuable effect in dealing with the problem of unemployment.
I want to deal briefly with the question of housing. We do not need housing in the metropolitan area of Toronto, and in other parts of Canada, simply to provide work, but it is doubtful whether there is any form of construction, meeting the needs of people, which would have a more valuable effect in dealing with the question of unemployment.
Yesterday, the Ontario federation of labour, meeting at Niagara Falls, produced a brochure for its 1,000 delegates in which it described Canada as a backward nation in the field of public housing, and spoke of the housing blight in Toronto as the worst in the province. It went on to say:
The Toronto situation is of course the worst in magnitude and here the municipal authorities as well as other levels of government have made the biggest headlines with the minimum of results.
This is not the occasion to go into great detail on what is required in the field of housing. In the area from which I come a badly needed change of policy would provide assistance from various levels of government for the rehabilitation and saving of existing housing, thus retarding its returning to a slum condition. In many other jurisdictions such financial support is available, and it has the effect of providing employment where it is needed.
If the government is serious about dealing with the problems of this large metropolitan area, and if it is also serious in seeking full employment, then I suggest the first thing it should do is get together with these other levels of government and make the plans necessary to meet these urgent needs of housing, rapid transit, and hospitals. If it would do that, then it would solve the problem of full employment, or at least go a long way towards solving it in that particular area.
I shall conclude my remarks by referring to a statement of policy approved by another political party, the British labour party, called "Labour and the Scientific Revolution." I know some people will say we should not listen to this because it is a socialist policy.
Unemployment Measures Lacking I suggest it makes good sense and I commend it to the government and members of the house. This is what it says:
In this new age of the computer and automation, as we can already see in the United States, the consequence of accepting rationalization and labour-saving techniques, whilst at the same time rejecting the need for central planning, is to abandon full employment. In short, planning without automation equals stagnation: automation without planning equals chronic unemployment.
From now on, we must frankly face the fact that any boy or girl who enters industry during the 1960's may well find his or her skill rendered obsolete more than once in the course of working life, with the result that a choice must be made between accepting whatever unskilled job is available or retraining in a new skill...
What we must develop, therefore,.. .is a completely new attitude to technological innovation and to redundancy as well...
This will require an enormous expansion of our adult training facilities. Both in the planning of this expansion program and in creating the new climate of opinion in industry which must accompany it, the trade unions will play a crucial role.
I suggest that all the training programs we have heard of, excellent though they are, do not constitute that enormous expansion of adult training facilities which is needed to cope with this problem.
The statement goes on to say:
As the scientific revolution proceeds, the wealth of the nation will increase and we shall be able not only to raise our own living standards but to contribute much more to the attack on world poverty___
The prospect that the scientific revolution opens before us is a working life which is secure and interesting, in a society where machines are subordinate to man; a world in which hardship and suffering are progressively eliminated and the whole range of man's culture is available to enrich the lives of us all. This is the true socialist vision which, in the past, want and ignorance have held from our grasp.
I do not apologize for the use of the word socialist. I think that is an apt description of it, and that is why we are proud in this party to call ourselves socialists and claim some part of this socialist vision.
But can we in fact break through the resistance and obstacles that confront us? We are confident that we can. In our factories and workshops we have perhaps the most skilled and mature working population in the world.
They are speaking of Britain, and what they say is true of Canada.
In our schools there is still a vast untapped potential of scientific and managerial skill. What is needed to meet the challenge of the scientific revolution is not a new scientific elite but a collective determination to succeed-and a government which will liberate the nation from its present frustrations so that together we can create a new and better Britain.
I substitute the word Canada for the word Britain, and suggest these words are applicable to Canada.
The reason I and other members of my party propose to support the amendment and

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is probably not too flattering for the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to hear it said, in this house, that he was not able to explain clearly the viewpoint of his party, and by one of his own followers at that.
In opening my remarks, I would like to borrow a few lines from the famed French fabulist, Jean de la Fontaine, and to adapt them to this debate. Paraphrasing his "Animals sick with the plague", I would say:
An evil which strikes terror in all hearts, and that an irate Providence invented to punish the crimes of the old parties,
Unemployment, if its name must be known."
Mr. Speaker, for two days now, you have seen that the old parties, Liberal as well as Conservative, are fully conscious of the problem they have had to put up with and have been unable to solve once in office. We have even seen the Conservative members hold the present Liberal administration, which came into office only a few months ago, entirely responsible for unemployment-there are approximately 250,000 unemployed at present in the country.
I should like to quote, if I may, for the information of the Conservative members and their leader in particular, some d.b.s. statistics for the years 1957-1958 and so on, when the country had a Conservative administration.
In 1957, there were 328,000 unemployed in this country, that is 5.7 per cent of the labour force; in 1958, there was a small improvement, because the Conservatives worked to stem unemployment:	579,000 jobless in
Canada, that is 9.7 per cent of the labour force; in 1959 there was an improvement:
578,000	unemployed, that is 9.5 per cent of the labour force; in 1960, there were 545,000 jobless, or 8.8 per cent of the labour force; and in 1961, the grand crowning-piece of the Conservative administration, we had 693,000 jobless, representing 10.8 per cent of the labour force.
Today, Mr. Speaker, here is the amendment introduced by the official opposition party:
"This house regrets the failure of the government to introduce any effective new policies or programs to reduce substantially unemployment in Canada, and in particular to alleviate winter unemployment, so as to achieve the promised full employment as undertaken in the Liberal party election promises."
I admit that the Liberal party as well as the Conservative party committed themselves, one after the other, during various election campaigns, to settle the unemployment problem; but of two evils, I choose the lesser because I do not want to go back to that

period when-in 1961-there were more than one million unemployed in this country and the Conservative government of that time could do nothing about it.
During the 1958 election campaign, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) said: I will not sleep as long as there is a man out of work in Canada.
Has he slept?
We do not know that but we know, Mr. Speaker, that many people were starving while he was awake.
That is why in 1962 and 1963 the Canadian people decided to choose a lesser evil-[DOT] but an evil just the same-to put an end to the ultimate shame of living in the country with the highest unemployment rate, as reported in Quebec city's Le Soleil on Wednesday, July 17, 1963:
Unemployment in Canada reached the highest rate in all the great industrial nations, even after the United States.
Mr. Speaker, if what is found in the amendment moved by the present Conservative party is all that is offered by way of a policy to check unemployment, we will not go along with that, because neither the Conservatives nor the Liberals have found real solutions to the unemployment problem in Canada today.
Mr. Speaker, all kinds of solutions are being suggested at the present time, those contained in the Gill report and those proposed by the present Minister of Labour in his offensive against unemployment.
If we briefly analyse those cures, we find that the Gill report proposes to amend the enforcement of the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to help the workers.
One readily realizes that this is merely a measure to relieve the present unemployed but not to prevent an increase in the number of jobless.
It is one thing to find work and another to give some assistance to unemployed workers.
I would even say that in certain areas unemployment insurance is no good, because it encourages unemployment, especially in those areas where salaries are low and it is felt that it is better to draw unemployment insurance than to work.
Among other remedial measures proposed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) there is the increase from 75 to 90 per cent in the federal assistance to vocational rehabilitation; this is a worthy and sound solution, but it will certainly not solve the present unemployment problem, at least for several years to come.
The Minister of Labour proposes to raise from 50 to 75 per cent the federal assistance
Unemployment Measures Lacking to the retraining of workers who are threatened with unemployment. We admit, Mr. Speaker, that such a step would somewhat palliate unemployment, in that workers displaced by automation would move to another community where a job may be waiting for them but, there again, that will do nothing to change the increasing number of new workers who enter the labour market, a situation which calls for the creation of at least 200,000 new jobs every year.
In general, the other suggested cures would only fill the existing gap; they do not take into account the labour surplus which will result from the increasing spread of automation.
Those measures are what I would call poultices. They remind me of the plugs which are used to patch up rusted piping and which only increase the pressure elsewhere in the pipe which has been weakened by rust.
As long as the Liberal government, just as the former Conservative government, will not realize that a piecemeal policy is not what is needed to solve unemployment, that an altogether new policy is necessary, because the present one is no longer suited to put to work the mass of the labour force available, we will continue to be faced with the same problem.
As long as the government refuses to tackle the underlying cause of the evil which gnaws at the labour force, we will not succeed in finding means to stem unemployment, as we would hope, and as is the case now in Germany where even 74-year old women work in stores as assistants while manpower is sought from everywhere.
In France, there is a shortage of manpower.
I wonder whether it would be possible on a continent as rich as America to find means of solving unemployment due to automation.
During last night's debates, we listened to a few suggestions, one of which astonished me. It came from a Social Credit member. Let me quote an extract from the speech made by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde) to the effect that one measure only could solve unemployment. Here is what he said:
I hope that taxes will be reviewed in order to And out means to give a new impetus, a new development to Canada, even if this would get our country in debt for the next ten years.
