Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Quebec West will allow me to

Unemployment Measures Lacking finish my remarks, he will understand my idea. I mean that this suggestion, even if it implies the present system, is bad, because it is not by increasing the national debt that Canadians will find relief. It is mostly by trying to reduce it that we will succeed. When Canadians pay less in taxes, taxes which serve only to pay interest on the national debt, taxes taken, in the final analysis, in the pockets of the taxpayers and which will deprive them, consequently, of an increased purchasing power, only then shall we be able to try really and stem unemployment.
A considerable increase in the redistribution of wealth within our country would create new jobs and even an improved standard of living.
A suggestion which bears a great resemblance to the Creditiste doctrine is the step taken recently in the United States by President Kennedy in order to reduce by 11 per cent direct income tax for the workmen and the American people. That measure will increase the purchasing power of American consumers, thus creating a demand for production, which in turn will increase employment and prevent unemployment. One is justified to wonder why there is no unemployment in wartime. The reason is that in wartime we experience an increased purchasing power, while in peacetime everything operates slowly and everybody then experiences a period of unemployment like the one we have had since the war and especially since the beginning of the Conservative administration in 1957.
The solution will only be found when measures dealing with developments in the automation century will have been understood and applied. Automation is getting more and more scientific and it will increasingly shove labour aside.
To advocate that to settle unemployment it is necessary to curb automation is false, because automation is the direct and beneficent result of the human mind in operation. In my opinion, if we curb automation, we thus curb the human mind in action.
We know that automation is the direct cause of unemployment, since it has supplanted the workers who were employed to produce what the machine now makes without them. All right. But the concern should not be that the worker will lose his job, but that as a result of his loss of income, he will no longer be able to buy the commodities that the machine will continue to produce. We are faced with this dilemma: either the machine goes on producing the goods that were produced by man in the past and that he could buy with the salary derived from his job, or we face up to the existing over production.
[Mr. Chapdelaine.l

The answer to the problem of automation is to make it possible for the workers to own the machines replacing them. In this way, man will be able to live on the goods produced by the machine which he owns, while at present, in opposition to this, production is increasing and the purchasing power is low and, according to all indications, will get lower and lower. The problem is not one of production but of distribution.
If only our present government, as well as other governments throughout the world would realize that it is not with second-class measures that we are going to solve the problem of unemployment, but by getting at the heart of the matter, that is the lack of purchasing power in the pockets of the consumers who alone can absorb the goods being produced; if only the government realized that it is not a question of greatly increasing the present money supply, if the government realized that such a thing could be done without printing money indiscriminately, as some people might have thought when somebody tried to explain the Social Credit doctrine by using the wrong terms, because those social allowances we have now might well be called dividends, then the government would be getting nearer to the Social Credit theory. But we do not believe you can provide everybody with a livelihood without taking into account the production capacity of this country.
If the government would understand that instead of leaving to the chartered banks the power they have at present to create 12 times as much money as they have on deposit in the Bank of Canada; if the government would gradually take back the power that we, Canadians, have given the chartered banks through the federal government for the operation of public services, little by little Canadians would have less money to pay back as interest on bonds and, as a result, the government would not have to levy so many taxes, which are used only to pay the interest on the public debt. The national debt has reached such a level that we have $900 million a year to pay as interest alone.
Let us just suppose for a moment that, in the country, Canadians no longer have to pay the government $900 million each year because that amount is no longer required to pay interest on the national debt, and let us suppose that the money were distributed as spending power.
That money would be left to the consumer in the form of purchasing power because it would not have been taken from him through taxes. Then you would see the Canadian economy moving again. And there would be

no need to dream up all kinds of second rate solutions to solve the unemployment problem.
I respectfully submit that these are not lunatic theories but indeed rather concrete theories forced upon us by reality and to be applied sooner or later. As a matter of fact, if we fail to do so, we will have to keep on borrowing and paying back, over periods of 20 to 30 years, for services we will have used but for which our children will have to pay because their fathers will not have been wise enough to put their affairs in order while they were living.
Mr. Speaker, I feel we might accept for the time being the measures submitted by the government. On the other hand, governments, whether Liberal or Conservative, will gradually have to reach the conclusion that a reform of Canada's monetary system is necessary if the economy is to develop normally in a country as rich as Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the question which has been debated since yesterday, namely that of unemployment, is one which follows naturally from a situation created by an obsolete economic system, by a system which is no longer suited to the present needs, and this precisely at the time when we speak of full employment, when we hear the representatives of the various political parties in this house speak of the ideal to be pursued, that is full employment, in brief, at the very moment when the number of unemployed is going up.
The hon. member who rose before me, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapde-laine) quoted a little while ago figures on the number of unemployed in Canada. He said that our country had respectively in 1959, 1960 and 1961, 578,000, 547,000 and 693,000 unemployed.
Now, last week, I put on the order paper question No. 1,469, which reads as follows:

"What was the value of goods and services produced for each of the last five years?"

And here is the answer I was given:
In 1958, the value of goods and services produced in Canada amounted to $36,048 million.
In 1959, it was $38,430 million, that is $2,400 million more than in 1958.
In 1960, at the time when Canada had
547,000	unemployed, the gross national product amounted to $39,437 million, that is an increase of $1 billion over the production of the preceding year.
In 1961, when our country held the unemployment or lack of employment record, our
Unemployment Measures Lacking gross national product reached $40,511 million, that is an increase of $1,100 million over the year 1960, although the number of unemployed reached the figure of 693,000.
In 1962, without any decrease in the number of jobs, the gross national product amounted to $43,646 million, that is an increase of $3,135 million over that of the preceding year.
Here we have an instance of the economical paradox in which we live, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, at the very moment when the situation of the unemployed remains unchanged, our national production is increasing, and that, without any participation of the arms and brains of our Canadian citizens. That is the problem confronting us today. At the very time when we hear some hon. members, even ministers and leaders of the opposition or of the government, talk about their good intentions with regard to unemployed Canadians, our national production is increasing while the number of the workless remains stationary, when it does not increase.
What solution is suggested? None whatsoever. At this time there is much talk of economic planning. We have no plans, no guidance, we lack government leadership in all spheres of economic life.
There is a lack of government leadership, while we are under pressure from various Canadian organizations, which ask us to intervene in a given sector of private enterprise, in a given field of our national production. The government is urged to make decisions for private enterprise, to levy more taxes on personal initiative, so as to be able to invade sectors where it should not step in at all.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde) mentioned yesterday the evidence given by Mr. Snyder, president of a large American industrial concern. He even quoted the concluding remarks of Mr. Snyder:
If we do not want to be up against a terrible unemployment crisis, within four or five years-
Since the article was written on October 5, 1963, that would take us to 1968.
If we do not want to be up against a terrible unemployment crisis within four or five years, it is important that teams of sociologists and economists-
Mr. Speaker, when I see the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) in his seat, I suggest to the government to mobilize the hon. minister and also the sociologists or economists who are members of the government team. I suggest to mobilize them not to let them sit in their place without offering any solution, but, as Mr. Snyder put it:
-teams of sociologists and economists to prepare drastic solutions to deal within an unprecedented problem.

Unemployment Measures Lacking
Mr. Speaker, we need drastic solutions, not bogus solutions. And what is that unprecedented problem? It is that automation will involve before long, in the United States, the elimination of 40,000 jobs each week. And we in Canada will feel the impact of that situation, even if it originates in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, it is not full employment which will offer a solution to the problem of automation, because it is evident that the more we use machinery, the greater the number of our unemployed people.
The question is to decide whether the use of machines in Canada is to penalize men, women and children or whether it should assist and serve the human person in Canada.
That is the question.
Mr. Speaker, why is it always necessary to offer the Canadian people a dish of oats as you would to horses to round them up in a corral? Why not enact legislation fitted to human needs?
Why not come up with bold solutions- and again this is where economists and sociologists would have an important role to play-since solutions half a century old can no longer meet the requirements?
This is neither 1867, 1912 or 1934 but 1963. Means of production have changed. There has been progress everywhere in the world except as far as the monetary system is concerned. In Canada and in other countries professing their respect of democracy, human rights and the right of every man to live decently in a country of his own, the monetary system has remained unchanged.
Mr. Speaker, it is our duty to create an economic context which would permit the accomplishment of the human personality and would make it possible for every human being to live his life according to his aspirations, and his talents. Then, we would see the whole of Canada achieve the high level of culture and the high standard of living sought by every Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, when the Social Crediters come up, in this house or outside, with a suggestion to boost the Canadian economy or even with something new, because we do need something new in Canada, and they maintain that the monetary system is without the shadow of a doubt what is preventing the economic recovery of this country today, they are right. Our monetary system is not adapted to the people's needs, and that is why, from one end of the country to the other, in all our provinces, we are faced with the same financial difficulties that prevent us from getting out of that rut that enslaves us.
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about monetary reform when the governments which have followed one another for the past 25 or 30

years have only been concerned with the reform of morals, institutions and private enterprise, with the interference of the left-wing and right-wing parties, the interference of the government with the people's way of life, the interference of the government with private property and private industrial planning.
Earlier, we have heard again a socialist colleague asserting that in order to boost our economy it was necessary to resort to socialism, planning, yokes and strait-jackets in Canada. We do not share that view. We believe that what exists in Canada today is not due to the initiative of the federal or the provincial governments but rather to free enterprise, to private planning which, in 1962, succeeded in creating in Canada a gigantic production of goods and services valued at $43 million. The government does not produce; on the contrary, it prevents production. And that is so true that recently it was decided to exempt from income tax any new corporation that would settle in underdeveloped or depressed areas.
Mr. Speaker, if the government does that, it is because it understands that private enterprise in Canada is now being taxed to the limit, and that is precisely the obstacle in the way of that economic development which this country needs at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, the monetary reform advocated by Social Credit is not at all mysterious.
A little while ago, the hon. member for Sherbrooke said that unemployment insurance is not much good. I agree, but when he goes on to say that unemployment insurance is an encouragement to laziness, then I do not agree with him. If there was no unemployment insurance at the present time, all our unemployed would literally starve in an immensely rich country.
Today, at noon, we heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) say that he had concluded a great sale of wheat to Poland. We made wheat sales to China, the U.S.S.R. and also Czechoslovakia, Mr. Speaker, but that did not create a single job in all Canada.
Why? Because, as I said, automation is the current problem. Now, as private enterprise and others in Canada use more and more machines instead of men, production will go on increasing year after year, and also the number of unemployed.
There is only one warranted and possible solution, and it is the following one: as machines, progress and science replace men at work, the government ought to order the Bank of Canada to give back to men, women and children a purchasing power which will enable them to buy what is produced by machines, progress and science. Then we will

respect the human person and at the same time machines, progress and science.
Mr. Speaker, the monetary reform proposed by Social Credit is extremely simple: to make financially possible what is physically realizable, desirable and morally good.
In that connection, a man very conversant with the monetary policies of Canada made a statement on October 24, 1963 or during the week of October 24. I am referring to a lecture by Mr. Louis Rasminsky, governor of the Bank of Canada, reported as follows in an article written by Mr. Laurent Lauzier of La Presse in Montreal:
At the beginning of the week, Mr. Louis Rasminsky, governor of the Bank of Canada, gave a most useful talk in which he explained the true role of monetary policy in the Canadian economy.
At this time when very different theories are being advocated concerning this delicate and complex question which seems to be the fundamental cause of the money crises our country has gone through, these past few years, it became imperative for this official to state the principles he follows in this field and to define the true meaning of monetary policy as an instrument to control our prosperity.
How can we speak of an instrument to control our prosperity when we have thousands and thousands of unemployed and needy families in Canada? And now we are being told about "an instrument to control our prosperity".
It must be admitted, Mr. Speaker, that the instrument to control our prosperity has unfortunately been a failure throughout Canada.
"The instrument to control our poverty" would be a more appropriate term in the circumstances.
Mr. Lauzier goes on to say in his article:
Mr. Rasminsky does not share the views of those who credit money management with a magic power, in the best as well as in the worst interests of our society. He gives it a much narrower scope. According to him, the monetary policy is not enough by itself to cure an economy beset with many ills, any more than a single medicine can succeed in restoring a sick person to health.
We appreciate this statement from the governor of the Bank of Canada. On the other hand, if the monetary policy alone is not sufficient to cure a deficient economy, what has the governor of the Bank of Canada to answer, for example, when we are asking the government to adopt more generous social measures.
What is lacking in Canada? Are we short of resources? Are we short of labour? No, we have from 500,000 to 600,000 unemployed. Are we short of brains, ability or goodwill? Mr. Speaker, we have all that in Canada. What we need, and the government is aware of it day after day, is money. We are suffering from a shortage of money and credit, from this chronic evil which prevents the
Unemployment Measures Lacking government from taking action to enable Canada to develop as it should in 1963.
Mr. Speaker, we have all that in Canada. But what is wrong, and the government realizes it more every day, is that it suffers from a chronic lack of money and credit, which prevents it from taking action to help Canada grow and prosper as it should in 1963.
And that is all Mr. Rasminsky's doing, that remarkable economist, chairman and governor of the Bank of Canada, who puts his nose into all sorts of things he does not seem to understand at all. But he can understand that monetary policy-
May contribute to correct a difficult situation-
There he admits that from 1929 to 1939, conditions were difficult for us. At that time we had thousands of unemployed in Canada, we had no social legislation, no family allowances and no old age pensions, in short we had no social security whatever, and the jobless were struggling along in abject misery at the time.
And in the years 1933-1934, when we had hundreds of thousands of unemployed, they destroyed wheat in western Canada, potatoes in eastern Canada, they threw thousands of bags of flour into the great lakes, milk into the sewers, and the same more or less happened all over Canada.
Now, at that time, the government had no solution. Yet suddenly, as if by magic-to quote Mr. Rasminsky-under the 1939 government and the leadership of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, they succeeded in finding millions of dollars to organize war and put Canada on a war footing overnight. As if by magic, the number of unemployed decreased and then vanished completely in Canada, as jobs were created by the war industries.
Is the situation today not equally urgent and does it not require that the problem be considered quite earnestly.
Mr. Rasminsky exclaims:
It can contribute to correct a difficult situation or act as a stimulating factor on the economy...
"Act as a stimulating factor". He admits that it can be a stimulating factor for the economy.
-when circumstances allow it.
Would the present circumstances not allow it? This is where Mr. Rasminsky forgets to state what are those circumstances.
-but it may show itself powerless and even inefficient if it is used to solve problems which are unrelated to its function.
Now, Mr. Speaker, all the problems today, and everyone knows it, are essentially financial problems.

In all fields where industry and the government want to take action, we are faced with a shortage of money.
There is no inflation at the present time in the country, it is rather deflation which is prevailing. Our production amounted to $43 billion in 1962, compared to a national income of approximately $32 billion. That is not inflation.
Inflation would be an inexistent production and at the same time an abundant purchasing power. That would be inflation. But when I think that we have no purchasing power and a production of $43 billion only for 1962, I say that we are living under deficit conditions and that there is deflation at present instead of inflation.

In other words, the governor of the Bank of Canada admits that the monetary policy is not a panacea.
We never stated that the monetary policy could graft a new leg onto a man with a wooden leg. We know that. It is not necessary in order to grasp that fact to have Mr. Ras-minsky's knowledge in monetary matters. Mr. Speaker, before the six o'clock adjournment, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) asked me whether there would still be unemployment if the Social Credit theory were applied. My answer is no and this is the reason why. Because of automation, the use of machinery and the progress of science, the unemployed would no longer be called "unemployed" but "retired". That is the difference between the present system we tolerate and the application of Social Credit principles.
What does Social Credit advocate? First of all, there is a reform of the monetary system to make the Bank of Canada the sole creator of new credit and to force the chartered banks to keep reserves equal to 100 per cent of the loans they make, as is the case at present for the caisses populaires. The banks would continue to lend exactly as at the present time, but instead of creating Active loans, they would lend their depositors' money. It would be something concrete and not mere figures as is the case today.
We suggest the setting up of a credit control board responsible for maintaining a perfect balance between money supply and outstanding credit on the one hand, and the gross national product on the other hand.
To maintain this balance, we suggest that a national dividend be distributed among all Canadian citizens. This dividend would be based on the difference between production on one hand and purchasing power on the other. That would not in the least create inflation,

but would establish a perfect balance between the purchasing power and the goods and services offered and produced in Canada. The payment of a dividend does not mean inconsiderate creation of money, without limit, but rather a dividend always closely related to the difference between production and purchasing power. This would then be social dividend because it would reach every individual in Canada and would be at the service of everyone. It would be socially besides being economically just.
Because of the consequences of automation, I do not see, Mr. Speaker, any other means to reach Canadian consumers, to enable them to purchase the things they need, the goods and services produced by the Canadian people.
That new purchasing power would not only do away with inflation but would always maintain a reasonable balance between, on the one hand, what consumers need to buy and, on the other hand, what producers have to offer to the consumers.
We are also suggesting a compensated discount to allow for an increase in purchasing power which would not necessarily amount to an increase in the money supply. Such a compensated discount was actually in force during the war years when the Liberal government of the day granted a two-cent a quart discount on milk, which was given to milk consumers and paid to milk producers or distributors.
Those are measures which are really different from what we have now. Those are measures which tend to bring a smile to the faces of those who have absolutely no solution to offer to deal with the present economic uneasiness.
Social Crediters feel they have that answer, and we are convinced that if economists of the Liberal party were to take the trouble of studying the proposals made by Social Credit, our national affairs could be run much more efficiently.
In the past, the Liberals as well as the Conservatives have beaten around the bush in a pitiful way within the framework of a system which no longer suits the needs of the nation.
Should we assimilate man, force him to put up with that system, or are we not duty bound to create a system which shows some respect for the individual?
Are systems meant to punish men or are they not designed to serve mankind?
If systems must exist to serve man, it is time that we, members of parliament, those responsible, took action.

ALLEGED PRIVILEGED POSITION OF CERTAIN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes left I will raise a very simple grievance. It relates to the situation that exists in the other place in so far as the holding of directorships, being consultants, or being held on retainer by certain companies, particularly certain finance companies, are concerned. My grievance is that we have at present a number of items on the order paper that have been referred to committee.
We also know from past experience one of the hon. gentlemen in the other place has tried to introduce legislation that would have something to do with making interest rates more clear and with setting a ceiling on them. I think it is unfair, unsound and undemocratic that people should have the opportunity to sit in judgment, and to scrutinize such legislation before it can become law, at the same time that they are either directors, presidents, consultants or held on retainers by some of the very companies going to be affected by such legislation.
My grievance is as simple as this. I want to draw it to the government's attention, in particular to the attention of the Prime Minister, because it is time we should consider this point very seriously, that implicitly built

into our parliamentary structure at the present time is a form of special privilege or lobbying that is to the advantage of certain corporate organizations that are able to retain members from the other place on their boards of directors or as legal retainers.
I suggest this form of lobbying should be brought out much more into the open, and the government and Prime Minister should consider some kind of legislation to put very strict limits on it. This point deserves real consideration, particularly because the house is now concerned with legislation relating to consumers finance.
I would appeal to backbenchers on the government side who have taken an interest in this, and who have also given some indication that they have liaison with their cabinet and Prime Minister, to consider how far this kind of legislation is going to get when you have the presidents of finance companies in the Senate and you have some senators who are under retainer from finance companies. I leave the grievance to sit in the minds of my Liberal friends, and in the Prime Minister's mind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has asked a very proper question. There was an understanding, or at least a declaration by the government at the time the house was good enough to extend the hours, that we would take a new department on each evening so that there would be an opportunity for every department to have some review before the end of the session, and so that hon. members would have an opportunity to bring up points with respect to every department of government. That is the reason we are following the course we are.
